sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Construction questions are about running a project: who is responsible for what, how long the work takes, what it costs and whether it is on track.

Scheduling and earned value questions are arithmetic once the network or the three cost figures are laid out clearly.
pitfalls: Mixing up the cost index (earned value over actual cost) and the schedule index (earned value over planned value).
Forgetting to convert thickness to the same unit as length and width in a quantity takeoff.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Construction Engineering Review Session 2022
items: Indemnification means one party agrees to cover another's losses from claims, usually including legal fees.
The pre-construction conference comes after award. A meeting before award is a different thing.
Submittals are product data, shop drawings and samples.
Trenches kill. OSHA requires a protective system at 5 ft (1.5 m) depth or more, and a competent person must inspect the excavation.
The engineer does not direct the contractor's means and methods. Work that does not conform is rejected through the owner.
Earned value is the budgeted cost of the work actually performed, not what was spent.
In a takeoff, convert inches to feet before multiplying.

bridge.keep: Quantities, unit costs and bid items, from engineer's estimates; reading plans and specifications.
rusty: Scheduling: critical path, float and precedence diagrams.
Equipment productivity and construction safety rates.
bridge.work: Planning-level and engineer's estimates, quantity take-offs from plan sheets, construction staging and traffic handling all draw on this topic.
bridge.exam: Scheduling and earned value are formula-driven and quick once the definitions are fixed in memory. They repay an hour of drill.

sections.title: Project administration
sections.body:
Project administration is the paperwork and relationships that hold a job together. The delivery method sets who contracts with whom. In design-bid-build the owner hires a designer, then bids the finished design to contractors. In design-build one entity does both. With a construction manager at risk, a builder advises during design and then guarantees a price.

The contract documents are the agreement, the general and special conditions, the drawings and the specifications. Bonds protect the owner: a bid bond, a performance bond and a payment bond. Changes go through change orders, and payment follows measured progress with retainage held back until completion.
pitfalls: Confusing a performance bond (the work gets finished) with a payment bond (subcontractors and suppliers get paid).
On select-all items, judging the list as a whole. Decide each option on its own.
Reading indemnification as covering any claim at all. It is tied to loss caused by the other party's negligence.

ideas.title: Who contracts with whom
ideas.text: In design-bid-build the owner holds separate contracts with the engineer, the contractor and usually the testing agency. The contractor holds the subcontracts and supply contracts. An inspector paid by the contractor would have a conflict of interest, which is why the owner hires the inspection.

ideas.title: Delivery method is not pricing
ideas.text: How the work is delivered (design-bid-build, design-build, construction manager) is a separate choice from how it is paid for (lump sum, unit price, cost plus).

ideas.title: Why design-build is faster
ideas.text: Construction of early work such as foundations can start while later work is still being designed. The price of that speed is that there is no finished design to bid, so there is no true lowest bid.

ideas.title: Retainage and lien releases
ideas.text: Retainage, commonly 5% to 10% of each payment, keeps the contractor engaged through the punch list. Lien releases are collected before final payment because an unpaid subcontractor can place a lien on the owner's property.

ideas.title: Delivery methods
ideas.text: Design-bid-build: the owner holds separate contracts with the designer and the contractor, in sequence. Design-build: one entity holds a single contract for both. Construction manager at risk: the manager commits to a guaranteed maximum price and holds the trade contracts. Agency construction management: the manager only advises.

ideas.title: Contract documents
ideas.text: The set is the agreement, the general and supplementary conditions, the specifications, the drawings and any addenda. Addenda change the documents before bids are opened; change orders change them after award.

ideas.title: Bonds
ideas.text: A bid bond guarantees the low bidder will sign the contract at the bid price. A performance bond guarantees the work will be completed. A payment bond guarantees subcontractors and suppliers will be paid.

ideas.title: Sequence of a job
ideas.text: Advertise, receive bids, award, notice to proceed, construction, substantial completion, punch list, final completion and final payment. Retainage is a share of each payment held back until the work is accepted.

ideas.title: Paper flow during construction
ideas.text: A request for information asks the designer to clarify the documents. A submittal or shop drawing shows how the contractor intends to meet them and is reviewed for conformance with the design intent, not for means and methods.

sections.deep:
Project administration is how a design becomes a built project under a contract. The delivery method decides who holds which contract and when the builder joins. The contract documents define the work, and a hierarchy of bonds, insurance and payment procedures manages the risk that a party fails to perform.

During construction the engineer's role is usually to interpret the documents, review submittals, observe the work and certify payment. Changes are made only through the contract's change procedure.
method: Identify the delivery method from who contracts with whom.
Identify the document that governs the question.
Match the risk to the bond or insurance that covers it.
Place the event in the project sequence from bid to closeout.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.

sections.title: Construction operations and methods
sections.body:
Operations questions are about getting work done safely and productively. Production is how much a machine or crew does per hour: the amount per cycle times the cycles per hour, reduced for the minutes actually worked. Match the fleet so that the loader and its trucks keep each other busy.

Safety comes first on site. OSHA sets rules for excavations, fall protection and equipment. Injury records are compared using an incidence rate per 200,000 hours worked. Temporary erosion controls such as silt fences and sediment basins keep soil on the site during construction.

formulas.name: Production rate
formulas.expr: volume per cycle × cycles per hour × efficiency

example.problem: A scraper carries 15 m^{3} per trip and makes a trip every 6 minutes, working 45 minutes per hour. Find its hourly production.

ideas.title: A loader and its trucks
ideas.text: Time to fill a truck is its capacity divided by the loading rate. A truck's cycle is fill plus haul, dump and return. The fleet moves (number of trucks × capacity × 60) / cycle time in minutes per hour, and can never beat the loader's own rate.

ideas.title: Erosion and sediment control
ideas.text: Silt fence, check dams, mulch, a stabilised entrance and a concrete washout keep sediment and wash water on the site during construction. They are temporary measures, distinct from the permanent stormwater system.

ideas.title: Trench safety
ideas.text: OSHA requires a protective system (sloping, shoring or a shield) for trenches 5 ft deep or more unless they are in stable rock, and a competent person must inspect the excavation.
Equipment production = volume per cycle × cycles per hour × efficiency. The efficiency factor (working minutes per 60) accounts for delays, operator breaks and repositioning.

ideas.title: Incidence rate
ideas.text: The OSHA incidence rate normalises injury counts to 200,000 hours, the hours worked by 100 full-time employees in a year (100 × 40 h × 50 weeks), so that firms of different sizes can be compared.

A balanced fleet has just enough trucks that one arrives as the loader finishes the previous one. The number is the truck cycle time divided by the loading time. Fewer trucks leave the loader idle; more leave trucks queuing.

examples.problem: An excavator has a 2.5 m^{3} bucket and a cycle time of 36 s. It works 50 minutes of each hour. What is its hourly production?
examples.idea: Equipment production = volume per cycle × cycles per hour × efficiency. The efficiency factor (working minutes per 60) accounts for delays, operator breaks and repositioning.
examples.steps:
Cycles per hour = 3,600 / 36 = 100.

Ideal production = 2.5 × 100 = 250 m^{3}/h.

Efficiency = 50 / 60 = 0.833.

Production = 250 × 0.833 = 208 m^{3}/h.

examples.problem: A contractor has 5 recordable injuries in a year in which employees worked 310,000 hours. What is the incidence rate per 200,000 hours?
examples.idea: The OSHA incidence rate normalises injury counts to 200,000 hours, the hours worked by 100 full-time employees in a year (100 × 40 h × 50 weeks), so that firms of different sizes can be compared.

examples.problem: A loader takes 5 minutes to fill a truck. Each truck needs 35 minutes for a full cycle including loading. How many trucks keep the loader working without waiting?
examples.idea: A balanced fleet has just enough trucks that one arrives as the loader finishes the previous one. The number is the truck cycle time divided by the loading time. Fewer trucks leave the loader idle; more leave trucks queuing.

sections.deep:
Construction operations are planned around the productivity of crews and equipment. Production is the volume moved per cycle times the cycles per hour times an efficiency factor. Fleets are balanced so that the loading unit and the hauling units keep each other busy.

Earthmoving must track the state of the soil, because a cubic metre in the bank swells when loosened and shrinks when compacted. Other common items are crane selection from load charts, formwork pressure, temporary structures and site safety.
method: Compute the cycle time and cycles per hour.
Multiply by capacity per cycle and the efficiency factor.
Convert volumes between bank, loose and compacted with swell and shrinkage factors.
Balance trucks to loader as truck cycle time over loading time.
Divide the quantity by production for duration.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.

sections.title: Project controls
sections.body:
Project controls track time and money against the plan. The critical path method lays the activities out as a network. A forward pass gives the earliest each can start and finish. A backward pass gives the latest. The difference is float. Activities with zero float form the critical path, and delaying any of them delays the project.

Earned value compares three figures: planned value (what should be done by now), earned value (the budgeted worth of what is done), and actual cost. The cost index is earned over actual. The schedule index is earned over planned. Below 1.0 is bad news in both.
pitfalls: Swapping PV and AC between the two indexes.
Counting an activity's whole budget as earned when it is only partly complete.

example.problem: A project has EV = $180,000 and AC = $200,000, with a total budget of $500,000. Find the CPI and the estimate at completion.

figure.caption: An activity-on-node network. The longest path, A-C-D, is critical; B has float.

ideas.title: The merge rule
ideas.text: Where paths join on the forward pass, an activity's early start is the largest early finish among its predecessors. On the backward pass, an activity's late finish is the smallest late start among its successors.

ideas.title: Compute earned value first
ideas.text: For each activity, earned value is percent complete times its budget. Both variances subtract from that total: schedule variance takes away the planned value and cost variance takes away the actual cost. An index below 1 is unfavourable.

ideas.title: CPM
ideas.text: In the critical path method the longest path through the network sets the project duration, and activities on it have zero float. Total float is the time an activity can slip without delaying the project: late start minus early start.

ideas.title: Earned-value analysis
ideas.text: Earned value management compares the budgeted value of work done (EV) with what it cost (AC) and with what was scheduled (PV). CPI = EV / AC; below 1.0 means over budget. SPI = EV / PV; below 1.0 means behind schedule.
Activity duration = quantity of work / (crew productivity × number of crews). Durations found this way feed the schedule network.

examples.problem: A project has four activities. A takes 4 days and starts the job. B takes 5 days and C takes 12 days; both follow A. D takes 3 days and follows both B and C. What is the total float of activity B?
examples.idea: In the critical path method the longest path through the network sets the project duration, and activities on it have zero float. Total float is the time an activity can slip without delaying the project: late start minus early start.
examples.steps:
Path A-B-D = 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 days. Path A-C-D = 4 + 12 + 3 = 19 days, which is critical.

B and C run in parallel between the same events, so B can slip by the difference: total float of B = 12 - 5 = 7 days.

examples.problem: At a status date a project has a planned value of $600,000, an earned value of $540,000 and an actual cost of $580,000. What is the cost performance index?
examples.idea: Earned value management compares the budgeted value of work done (EV) with what it cost (AC) and with what was scheduled (PV). CPI = EV / AC; below 1.0 means over budget. SPI = EV / PV; below 1.0 means behind schedule.

examples.problem: A crew places 45 m^{2} of formwork per day. There are 1,620 m^{2} to place and 3 crews working. How many working days are needed?
examples.idea: Activity duration = quantity of work / (crew productivity × number of crews). Durations found this way feed the schedule network.
examples.steps:
Daily output = 3 × 45 = 135 m^{2}/day.

Duration = \frac{1,620}{135} = 12 working days.

sections.deep:
Project controls measure whether the job is on time and on budget. The critical path method builds a network of activities, makes a forward pass for early dates and a backward pass for late dates, and reports float as the difference. The longest path is critical and has zero float.

Earned value analysis puts progress in dollars. Planned value is what should have been done by now, earned value is the budget for what has been done and actual cost is what it cost. Their differences and ratios give schedule and cost variances and indices, and the indices forecast the cost at completion.
method: Draw the network with durations.
Forward pass: early finish = early start + duration; a successor's early start is the largest early finish of its predecessors.
Backward pass: late start = late finish - duration; a predecessor's late finish is the smallest late start of its successors.
Total float = late start - early start.
For earned value, compute SV = EV - PV, CV = EV - AC, SPI = EV / PV, CPI = EV / AC.

sections.title: Construction estimating
sections.body:
An estimate prices a job before it is built. Start with a quantity takeoff: measure every item from the drawings in its pay unit, such as cubic metres of concrete or square metres of formwork. Multiply each quantity by a unit cost that covers labor, material and equipment.

Add indirect costs: site overhead, home office overhead, contingency and profit. Allow for waste on materials. Early estimates use cost per square metre or per unit. Detailed estimates price each item.
pitfalls: Mixing millimetres and metres in a takeoff.

example.problem: A footing 2 m by 2 m by 0.5 m is poured 12 times. With 4% waste, how much concrete is ordered?

ideas.title: Takeoff habits
ideas.text: Measure walls and wall footings along their centreline perimeter and slabs by their inside dimensions, and remember the isolated footings. Concrete in cubic feet divided by 27 gives cubic yards. Steel is weight per foot times length times the number of pieces, divided by 2,000 for tons.

ideas.title: Labour cost
ideas.text: Man-hours are the productivity (hours per unit) times the quantity. Cost is man-hours times the wage, increased by the labour burden for taxes, insurance and benefits.
Quantity takeoff for concrete is the neat volume from the drawings, increased by a waste allowance for spillage, over-excavation and uneven subgrade. Convert the thickness to metres first.
A bid item price is its direct cost (quantity × unit cost) plus a markup that covers overhead and profit.
Formwork is measured as contact area, the surface of concrete that touches the forms. A wall has two faces, so the contact area is 2 × length × height (ends ignored here).
Work in feet, then convert. A thickness in inches is divided by 12, and cubic feet are divided by 27 to give cubic yards.
Steel is taken off by weight: weight per foot times length times the number of pieces. Divide pounds by 2,000 for short tons.
Labour-hours are productivity times quantity. Cost is hours times wage, increased by the labour burden that covers payroll taxes, insurance and benefits.

examples.problem: A slab on grade is 40 m long, 25 m wide and 175 mm thick. Allowing 7% for waste, how much concrete should be ordered?
examples.idea: Quantity takeoff for concrete is the neat volume from the drawings, increased by a waste allowance for spillage, over-excavation and uneven subgrade. Convert the thickness to metres first.

examples.problem: A job needs 1,600 m^{3} of excavation at a direct cost of $11.5 per m^{3}. Overhead and profit add 16%. What is the bid price for this item?
examples.idea: A bid item price is its direct cost (quantity × unit cost) plus a markup that covers overhead and profit.

examples.problem: A concrete wall is 32 m long and 4.5 m high. What area of formwork is needed to form both faces?
examples.idea: Formwork is measured as contact area, the surface of concrete that touches the forms. A wall has two faces, so the contact area is 2 × length × height (ends ignored here).

examples.problem: A slab is 80 ft long, 36 ft wide and 7 in thick. How many cubic yards of concrete does it contain?
examples.idea: Work in feet, then convert. A thickness in inches is divided by 12, and cubic feet are divided by 27 to give cubic yards.

examples.problem: A floor has 18 steel beams, each 32 ft long, of a shape that weighs 44 lb per foot. What is the total weight of the beams in tons?
examples.idea: Steel is taken off by weight: weight per foot times length times the number of pieces. Divide pounds by 2,000 for short tons.

examples.problem: Erecting steel takes 9.0 labour-hours per ton. A job has 60 tons, the average wage is $44 per hour and the labour burden is 32%. What is the labour cost?
examples.idea: Labour-hours are productivity times quantity. Cost is hours times wage, increased by the labour burden that covers payroll taxes, insurance and benefits.

sections.deep:
An estimate prices the work from quantities. The quantity takeoff measures each item from the drawings: volumes of concrete and earth, areas of formwork and paving, weights of steel. Unit costs for labour, material and equipment are applied, and indirect costs, overhead, contingency and profit are added to reach the bid.

Estimates become more accurate as design progresses, from order-of-magnitude figures based on cost per unit of capacity to detailed estimates from complete drawings. Cost indices adjust historical costs for time and location.
method: Measure the quantity in the unit the cost is quoted in.
Add waste, laps or swell allowances.
Multiply by unit cost; build unit cost from crew rate over productivity when needed.
Add overhead and profit as percentages.
Adjust old costs with the ratio of cost indices.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.work: The same take-off and unit-price logic as an engineer's estimate, with waste, swell and productivity made explicit.

sections.title: Interpretation of engineering drawings
sections.body:
Drawings are the language of construction. A plan looks straight down. An elevation looks at a face. A section slices through to show what is inside. Details enlarge a small area. A scale relates a length on paper to a length on the ground.

On site plans, contour lines join points of equal elevation: close together means steep, and contours bend upstream where they cross a valley. Profiles show elevation along a route, with stations marking distance. Symbols, line types and abbreviations are explained in the legend and general notes, which govern along with the specifications.

formulas.name: Scale
formulas.expr: ground length = drawing length × scale factor

pitfalls: Reading a scale of 1:200 as 200 mm per metre. It means 1 unit on paper is 200 units on the ground.

example.problem: Contours at a 2 m interval are 25 m apart in plan. Find the slope.

ideas.title: Areas from scaled drawings
ideas.text: At 3/4 in = 1 ft, convert each measured dimension to its real length first, then multiply. Scaling the paper area directly needs the scale factor squared, which is where mistakes happen.

ideas.title: When documents disagree
ideas.text: Contract documents state an order of precedence. Later, more specific documents such as addenda generally govern over earlier, more general ones. Only the professional who sealed a drawing may change it.
An engineer's scale states how many feet on the ground one inch on the drawing represents. Ground distance = drawing distance × scale.
A ratio scale of 1:n means one unit on the drawing is n of the same units in reality. Multiply by n, then convert millimetres to metres.
Convert each drawing dimension to its real length before multiplying. At 3/4 in to the foot, real feet = drawing inches / 0.75.

examples.problem: On a plan drawn at a scale of 1 in = 30 ft, a property line measures 4.75 in. How long is the line on the ground?
examples.idea: An engineer's scale states how many feet on the ground one inch on the drawing represents. Ground distance = drawing distance × scale.

examples.problem: A drawing is at a scale of 1:200. A wall measures 47 mm on the drawing. How long is the wall?
examples.idea: A ratio scale of 1:n means one unit on the drawing is n of the same units in reality. Multiply by n, then convert millimetres to metres.

examples.problem: On a drawing at a scale of 3/4 in = 1 ft, a room measures 13.50 in by 8.25 in. What is the actual floor area?
examples.idea: Convert each drawing dimension to its real length before multiplying. At 3/4 in to the foot, real feet = drawing inches / 0.75.

sections.deep:
Engineering drawings are a language with fixed conventions. Plans look down, elevations look sideways and sections cut through. Scales relate drawing length to real length. Contours show the shape of the ground, and profiles show elevations along an alignment with the vertical scale exaggerated.

Reading drawings for the exam means extracting quantities and relationships: lengths from scales, slopes from contours, cut and fill from a profile, member sizes and reinforcement from details and schedules.
method: Find the scale and north arrow.
Convert drawing measurements to real lengths with the scale.
Read contours: the interval gives the elevation change, the spacing gives the slope.
On profiles, read elevations and stations separately from their own scales.
Cross-reference details and schedules for sizes.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.work: Scales, contours and sections are read exactly as on your own plan sheets.
